# The Latter Cloud

<margin>Married women</margin> <note>original: "sīmantinīnām"</note>. According to the Amarakosa <note>a famous Sanskrit thesaurus</note>: "Woman, married woman, bride." <margin>Brought by a friend</margin> <note>original: "suhṛdupanataḥ"</note>. This means received from a friend or through the mouth of a friend. The word "friend" is used here to prevent any suspicion of a secret lover during their separation. The news <note>original: "udantaḥ"</note> of her beloved. According to the Amarakosa: "News, report, account, and tidings are synonyms." It is "slightly less" <note>original: "kiṃcidūnaḥ"</note> than an actual meeting with the beloved, meaning it brings almost as much joy as his physical presence.

Now he delivers the message:

"O long-lived one! On my behalf and to benefit yourself, speak thus to her: 'Your companion, staying in the hermitages of Ramagiri, is alive. Separated from you, he asks after your welfare, O fragile one! For this is the very first thing to be said to living beings for whom calamities are so common.'" — Verse 41

Regarding the phrase "O long-lived one" <note>original: "āyuṣman"</note>: the suffix implies praise, meaning "one whose life is praiseworthy because of service to others." "On my behalf" <note>original: "mama vacanāt"</note> refers to my request. "To benefit yourself" <note>original: "ātmana upakartum"</note> means to make your own life meaningful through helping others. Although "yourself" is the object of the act of helping, the use of the genitive case <note>a grammatical case indicating possession or relation</note> is not incorrect, as it merely expresses a general relation. As Bharavi <note>a famous 6th-century poet</note> says: "That wealth is beneficial which belongs to others." Similarly, Sriharsha <note>the poet of the Naishadha Charita</note> writes: "To benefit the virtuous, to see the Goddess of Fortune, to travel through the sky." Therefore, the statement of the commentator Natha <note>an earlier commentator on Kalidasa</note> that the second case <note>accusative</note> is sometimes seen elsewhere is simply his own opinion.

Speak "thus" to my beloved. What should be said? "O fragile one <note>original: "abale"</note>, your companion and husband resides in the hermitages of Ramagiri." "Alive" <note>original: "avyāpannaḥ"</note> means he has not died. He gives the reason for not dying: "Separated" <note>original: "viyuktaḥ"</note>, meaning though he suffers from separation, he "asks after your welfare" <note>original: "kuśalaṃ pṛcchati"</note>. Because of the nature of the verb "to ask," it takes two objects. Indeed, for living beings whose "calamities are common" <note>original: "sulabhavipadām"</note>—meaning misfortunes occur without effort—this very welfare is the "first thing to be said" <note>original: "pūrvābhāṣyam"</note> or the first thing that must necessarily be asked. The suffix used here denotes necessity.

With his body, your slender body; with his deeply burning body, your burning body; with his tearful body, your body flowing with tears; with his incessantly longing body, your longing body...

<margin>1. Long-lived one. 2. He should speak. 3. One. 4. Separated (feminine), joined. 5. First to be said to those for whom calamities are common; for in the case of perishable instruments of living beings, this is the first breath. 6. O fair-bodied one, and slender. 7. Flowing with tears.</margin>

<summary>This page contains a Sanskrit commentary on verse 41 of the Meghaduta, where the Cloud messenger is instructed on how to approach the Yaksha's wife. It explains the grammatical nuances of the address and emphasizes that checking on someone's welfare is the essential first step in communication between mortals.</summary>
<keywords>Meghaduta, Kalidasa, Mallinatha, Sanskrit grammar, Ramagiri, welfare, separation, Amarakosa, Bharavi, Sriharsha</keywords>
